summary: This Wikipedia-derived note gives an overview of Estonia, covering its independence history, sport, politics, geography, religion, WWII occupation, historical subdivisions and demographics, defence cooperation, and economy. It traces Estonia's path from the Singing Revolution and the 1991 restoration of independence through closer Nordic ties to EU membership and adoption of the euro in 2011.
one_line: Overview of Estonia's history, politics, geography, religion, sport, defence ties and economy, from independence in 1991 to euro adoption in 2011.
key_facts: On 20 August 1991, Estonia declared formal independence during the Soviet military coup attempt in Moscow, reconstituting the pre-1940 state.
The Soviet Union recognised the independence of Estonia on 6 September 1991.
The Estonian Sovereignty Declaration was issued on 16 November 1988.
In 1989, more than two million people formed the Baltic Way human chain through Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia.
Estonia first competed as a nation at the 1920 Summer Olympics, although the National Olympic Committee was established in 1923.
Estonia's best Olympic results were 13th in the medal table at the 1936 Summer Olympics and 12th at the 2006 Winter Olympics.
Andrus Ansip was Europe's longest-serving Prime Minister, serving from 2005 until 2014.
Estonia's constitution guarantees freedom of religion and separation of church and state.
The Eurobarometer Poll 2005 found that only 16% of Estonians profess a belief in a god, the lowest of all countries studied.
The Republic of Estonia was established on 24 February 1918.
In January 1944, a radio address by the last legitimate prime minister asked able-bodied men born from 1904 through 1923 to report for military service, resulting in around 38,000 new enlistments.
Estonia was incorporated into the German province of Ostland during the German occupation.
Reval (Tallinn) was granted Lübeck city rights in 1248 and joined the Hanseatic League.
Estonia adopted the euro on 1 January 2011 and became the 17th eurozone member state.
In 2015, Estonia's GDP (PPP) per capita was $28,781 according to the IMF, and the country was ranked 8th in the Index of Economic Freedom.
